title: Sustainer of all

segments.voice: Yesterday, ghat ghat, and your line: every heart. The Master of all beings, found inside each one; today, who feeds them.

Split a rock in a field, and sometimes there's a tiny creature living inside: a beetle in a damp hollow, a grub, a pale little worm. Nobody brings it groceries. Nobody checks on it. And yet there it is, alive, with what it needs. Guru Arjan, the same Guru who wrote Sukhmani, used exactly that picture in a hymn Sikhs recite every evening, and it's the picture under today's line from the twenty-second ashtpadi.
screen: `A CREATURE INSIDE A ROCK.` → `NOBODY BRINGS IT GROCERIES.` → `THE SUSTAINER OF ALL.`

segments.voice: The twenty-second ashtpadi, which began by naming God the Master of all beings, says that God sustains each one of them. The word Sikhs often use for that sustenance is rijak: daily bread, livelihood, what keeps a creature alive. Guru Arjan unfolds the idea in a hymn in raag Gujri that's part of Rehras, the evening prayer. In paraphrase: why, mind, do you scheme and worry, when God Himself is busy caring for you? Even in rocks and stones He made creatures, and set their food before them. Then a second picture. A migrating crane flies hundreds of kos, the old measure of distance, leaving her young behind. Who feeds them? Who teaches them to eat? Have you never thought of that? The chicks alone, the mother far away, and still they're fed. Now, what this teaching isn't. It isn't a promise that no one will ever go hungry, and it isn't permission to stop working. Sikhs are taught kirat karni, honest work, and langar feeds whoever comes, because people do go hungry; Sikhs see feeding them as God's work done through human hands. The point is about worry. Guru Arjan isn't telling the mind to stop trying. He's telling it to stop scheming and fretting as if everything depended on it alone. And often, Sikhs would say, the way God feeds someone is through you.
screen: `RIJAK: WHAT KEEPS A CREATURE ALIVE.` · `IN ROCKS AND STONES, FOOD SET OUT.` · `THE CRANE FLIES; THE CHICKS ARE FED.` · `NOT A REASON TO STOP WORKING.` · then, large: `HE FEEDS ALL.`

segments.voice: If you have a pet, give it a little food or fresh water now, slowly; if not, put a few crumbs on a windowsill or water a plant, then sit and breathe. Watch, or picture, the creature receiving it, and notice that for this moment you're part of how it's sustained. If you pray, say Waheguru as you give.
Rijak, sustenance or livelihood: Sukhmani says God sustains each creature with its rijak; Guru Arjan pictures food set out even in rocks, and a crane's chicks fed while she's far away.
Your line: he feeds all. The worry can loosen its grip. Day five hundred twenty-four counts.

howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib hear that God sustains every creature, and each evening in Rehras recite Guru Arjan's hymn picturing food set out even for creatures within rocks.

chat.says: Money's tight. Does trusting God to feed us mean I can stop working and just wait?
options: No. Guru Arjan says drop the scheming and fretting, not the work; Sikhs keep honest work too.
Yes. The hymn promises no one ever goes hungry, so effort really isn't needed.
No. It means every meal is earned by you alone, so God isn't part of it at all.
chat.meaning: The hymn speaks to worry, not work: stop scheming as if everything depended on you alone. Sikhs are taught kirat karni, honest work, alongside the trust.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): the hymn says sai kosaa, hundreds of kos, not miles; voice and fork now say kos. Cut 'a picture many Sikhs love'. Langar is no longer said to exist only because of hunger, and the odd langar myth is replaced with one the teach clears up (the hymn is not a promise that no one goes hungry). Pronunciation changed to RIJ-uk, the usual Punjabi sound; a Keeper should confirm.
